articles.content:
​W​e had years of trainerflation​ but now value ​and versatility are back in fashion

W hen Nike’s Air Max 95 trainers first landed in Britain back in the mid-1990s, they looked unlike anything else. Created by footwear designer Sergio Lozano, the shoe had wavy layers running down its sides, neon yellow accents, and visible ‘Air’ bubbles underfoot. But in the UK, one detail quickly became as famous as the shoe itself: its £110 price tag.

The Air Max 95 immediately picked up the nickname “110” because spending £110 on trainers seemed outrageous at the time. Owning a pair quickly became a status symbol among young men across Britain , while in celebrity circles they were worn by everyone from Jay-Z to Kylie Minogue.

Over 30 years later, £110 looks relatively modest next to the upper end of the market catering to trainer enthusiasts. In a pretty neat example of trainerflation, flagship running shoes from Nike, New Balance, and Adidas easily retail for between £200 and £250.

For Dom Jacob, founder of sneaker discovery platform Sneak in Peace , the story begins during the 2020 pandemic. “During Covid, the low end of the sneaker market went up massively in price,” he says. “Nike and Adidas and the rest worked out they were missing the profit on their own product, because resale websites like StockX and GOAT were taking it.”

The resale boom changed what trainers meant. Limited releases weren’t simply shoes any more. They became assets to flip, and brands watched a growing slice of the money end up in somebody else’s pocket. In 2020, for example, the average Nike SB Dunk Low was reselling for more than £400, several times what many pairs originally cost at retail.

“There was a lot of greed during that period,” Jacob says. “[Trainer brands] cut the quality down while they raised the prices. The price of a sneaker became disconnected from what it was actually worth to the person buying it.”

Now, though, there are signs trainer enthusiasts are quietly pushing back. They’re buying fewer pairs, keeping old ones for longer, and getting excited about trainers that don’t cost £250 in the first place.

Nike’s V5 RNR costs £80. The New Balance 740 can be picked up for £70, the Asics Gel-1130 retails for about £90, and Adidas has plenty of trainers below the £90 mark. These aren’t being hidden away as entry-level options either. They’re front and centre in campaigns and on shop floors. And sneakerheads are actually buying into them. Jacob points to the success of Nike’s slide £79.99 Mind 001, which he says remained sold out for seven months , as proof that lower-priced trainers can generate just as much excitement as considerably more expensive releases.

Mikey Clarke, an app developer, has been collecting trainers for over a decade and remembers the days of the Nike “110”. “That felt expensive at the time, but it was attainable if you saved up,” he says. “Now I think harder before buying anything because prices have gone up so much. If I’m spending that kind of money, the shoe has to do everything rather than just being a nice addition to the collection.”

Fashion falling for relatively affordable trainers isn’t new. In 2010, designer Phoebe Philo helped turn the Adidas Stan Smith – then a simple £70-ish tennis shoe – into one of fashion’s most wanted trainers when she wore them to take her catwalk bow. Soon, seemingly everyone had a pair. More recently, the £95 Samba went from a humble indoor football shoe to one of the biggest trainers in fashion before the former PM Rishi Sunak killed them .

What’s different now is the reason we’re reaching for cheaper shoes. In 2026, value itself is becoming part of the appeal. Household budgets have tightened, and the resale bubble has burst. Suddenly, shoppers are asking a question sneaker brands haven’t really had to answer for years: is this actually worth the money?

Crucially, it isn’t people who have always bought cheaper trainers driving the shift, it’s enthusiasts who previously thought nothing of spending £250 on a pair. For them, getting excited about an £80 Nike represents a pretty significant change.

Jacob believes trainers are returning to what they were always meant to be. “We have come back to the daily runner,” he says. “You can do your morning jog in it if you really need to, and go straight to the supermarket afterwards.” That crossover matters: one pair that can handle a light run and everything else you do that day suddenly starts looking like better value.

There are thriftier ways to deal with trainerflation too. Vinnie Tao, founder of Manchester-based shoe care boutique Sneaker Pharm, has noticed more customers choosing to repair worn-out pairs rather than replace them. “I think that’s being driven by a combination of economics and sustainability,” he says.

The £200 trainer isn’t going anywhere. But after years of convincing trainer enthusiasts to spend more, sportswear brands are remembering something they knew all along: affordable doesn’t necessarily have to mean undesirable.

articles.title: Experts battling extinctions after record heat
articles.summary: Scientists are studying the plight of six species of butterfly and plant affected by the heatwaves.
articles.content:
Many species are struggling to cope in what has been the UK's hottest-ever summer

Scientists hope to prevent the extinction of some rare species by trying to understand their changing needs, as the UK nears the end of its hottest-ever summer.

Using money from Natural England and the Crown Estate, the Royal Entomological Society is working with other groups to update conservation guidance for grassland sites in Gloucestershire, Somerset and Wiltshire to study our changing climate.

"Urgent adaptations are needed to mitigate the effects of successive heatwaves on plants and the insects that rely on them to thrive," the society said.

It comes as elsewhere, wetlands created at the National Trust's Holnicote Estate have helped to store water, reduce flooding, and boost wildlife.

The society said climate change has accelerated dramatically since some of the current habitat management guidance was written.

The six species at the centre of the project are found in lowland chalk grassland, an internationally rare habitat. They are the large blue butterfly, the Duke of Burgundy butterfly, the marsh fritillary butterfly, the wart-biter cricket, juniper and the burnt-tip orchid.

The project hopes to establish how six species are coping and prevent their extinction

David Simcox FRES, Conservation Project Manager at the Royal Entomological Society, said: "As many of us cope with another spell of extreme weather, it's easy to forget that our wildlife is experiencing exactly the same pressures.

"Some of the habitat management guidance we still rely on was written over 20 years ago and our understanding - and the rate of climate change - has moved on enormously since then.

"By combining decades of long-term research with new science, this project will help us understand how six key endangered species are responding to a changing climate and provide practical guidance to support their recovery."

This year is the first on record when 35C (95F) has been reached in three different calendar months. It was also the driest July in England and Wales since records began 190 years ago.

Stuart McCarthy-Thompson, who works at the Avon Wildlife Trust, said the impact has been "devastating".

"Plants are desiccated, the grassland is pretty much gone and there's been a lot of soil erosion as well. We're also seeing a lot of trees that are quite stressed - losing leaves and their fruit."

Beavers have helped part of the Holnicote Estate remain green and lush, despite this summer's drought

One success story however comes from the Holnicote Estate in Somerset, where the introduction of beavers to create wetlands has helped the area remain green and lush despite this summer's drought.

The National Trust said the scheme showed the value of "nature-based solutions", in which natural features such as rivers connected with floodplains and wildlife including beavers are used to deliver benefits for landscapes and people.

Ben Eardley, project manager at Holnicote, said: "For generations as a nation we've drained wetlands, straightened rivers and moved water off the land as quickly as possible.

Updating the conservation guidance is one of 130 projects being funded through Natural England's £60m Species Recovery Programme, as part of the Wild Again: Restoring England's Wildlife initiative, the largest-ever UK government investment in wildlife recovery.

articles.title: 'I've caught one fish all season' - how a polluted river could end 300 years of coracle fishing
articles.summary: The tradition on a Carmarthenshire river once fished by US President Jimmy Carter could be coming to an end.
articles.content:
Andrew Davies and Keith Elias worry that the tradition of coracle fishing could be coming to an end

It is a centuries-old tradition in Wales, but coracle fishers on a major river have said pollution has meant there are "no fish" left.

Testing by campaign group Save the River Tywi showed evidence of industrial, agricultural and human waste pollution, with fishers saying they often see dead fish bobbing up and down in the water.

One fifth-generation coracle fisherman described the situation in Carmarthenshire as "dire" after only catching one fish in the three-month season between May and July.

Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said it took all reports of pollution seriously and had "a number of ongoing enforcement and compliance investigations within the Tywi catchment".

Keith's great-grandfather, William Elias - pictured here with Keith's cousin Malcolm - would make coracles

The tradition of coracle fishing has been part of life on the Tywi for centuries.

Typically done at night, fishermen use small rounded boats with nets cast among them to catch salmon and sewin [sea trout].

It was once an important livelihood in west Wales, but today it is mostly a heritage tradition, rather than a full-time source of income.

US President Jimmy Carter even loved fishing in these rivers , but according to fishermen, recent pollution has made it impossible.

Chairman of Carmarthen Coracle and Netsman Association, Andrew Davies, said he thought the four coracle men on the Tywi had caught 12 fish among them in the whole of the 2026 season when, a few years ago, "you'd catch that many in a night".

Keith's uncle, grandfather and great-grandfather were all coracle fishermen on the Tywi

Keith Elias's family have been fishing on the river for 300 years - he said he had only caught one fish this season.

"It's been in my family for so long, I love carrying the tradition on, but it's getting to the point where you get to the end of the season and you're not hitting fish.

Last year, the nearby River Teifi had been noted as one of the UK's most polluted rivers , with 2,232 spills lasting more than 22,000 hours recorded in 2024.

It has been reported that some incidents of pollution were made by Welsh Water .

The company said it would invest £889m on storm overflows between 2025 and 2030, including six projects to reduce their impact on the Tywi.

It added: "We are determined to play our part to improve river water quality on the Tywi, but this isn't just an issue for water companies, collaboration is needed across sectors, including industry and agriculture, to ensure improvements."

Local people have also shared videos online of discharge across the river, which they claim appear to be from a nearby electronics recycling company Mekatek.

Mekatek said it shared concerns about the drop in sewin and had spent more than "40 years developing and improving our processes to ensure we are not a factor in that reduction".

It added: "Anyone wishing to understand what we do and how well we do it is more than welcome to arrange to visit the site and view our operations for themselves."

Fishermen on the River Tywi say they often find dead fish floating in the water

"I've been fishing for 38 years, I've never seen a season as bad as this," he said.

"When I first started, this river was black with fish, it was alive with fish. But it's gone now - there's no life in the river."

He said only four fishing licences had been taken out this year, compared with 12 when he started: "People have just, I won't say given up, but the enthusiasm's gone."

He said that the bad smell coming from the river "doesn't help" and he and others had reported cases of pollution to NRW "all the time", but "nothing seems to be done".

"I think something needs to be done to clean the rivers up in Wales, people have been dodging the bullet," he said.

Citizen scientists on behalf of Save the River Tywi, who have been conducting tests on the river, said there had been evidence of pollution coming from farms, companies based along the river and people.

Mayor of Carmarthen Russell Sparks said the river had been in a "really tough situation".

He added: "Over the last couple of years it's been really sad to see it, feel it and smell it."

Sparks said the smell was a combination of pollutants and algae blooms "creating this negative cycle".

In July the annual Tywi River Festival had to be cancelled because of the pollution, which Sparks said left people "absolutely devastated".

The mayor of Carmarthen automatically takes up the ancient role of Admiral of the Port and Sparks said it "breaks his heart" that his time in the role may see the end of coracle fishing.

With fishermen only catching "six sewin last year, there's a strong possibility that they won't take up their licenses next year".

Carmarthenshire MP Ann Davies wants "firmer action taken" against those who "constantly pollute the river".

She also said - as someone who farms herself - farmers have a responsibility to not pollute the river, along with people and businesses.

"We have a collective responsibility on what we buy, what we flush down the toilet."

Huwel Manley, head of south-west operations for NRW, said "Like many rivers, the Tywi faces a range of environmental pressures, including pollution and is also impacted by the current dry weather conditions which are seeing an increase in the water temperature along with wider ecological challenges.

"We take all reports of suspected pollution seriously. We currently have a number of ongoing enforcement and compliance investigations within the Tywi catchment, including cases that are progressing towards court proceedings."

The Welsh government said: "The Tywi is one of Wales' most important rivers, supporting internationally important habitats and species, local communities, recreation and cultural traditions such as coracle fishing."

It had been "aware of recent concerns regarding foam, odours and discolouration in the River Tywi" and "NRW have investigated and confirmed the impacts were linked to natural environmental conditions".

It said NRW had been investigating a separate potential source of pollution entering the Tywi and as those investigations remain ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further.

articles.title: I’ll admit it: I’ve cycled through red lights. But Britain’s traffic laws are to blame, not me | Simon Jenkins
articles.summary: The essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rules I plead guilty. I have loved and used the streets of London all my life, as a cyclist, driver and pedestrian. Touch wood, I have done so without accident, blemish or insurance claim. Yet now I find myself perpetually on the wrong side of the law. Regulation has become bureaucratic and chaotic. When I try to drive at the authorised speed of 20mph on many through roads, I am hooted at and overtaken by vans, cars, coaches and buses. And when I sit dutifully on my bike at a traffic light, I am jostled by swarms of cyclists riding through on red, furious at being treated as if they were car drivers. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...
articles.content:
The essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rules

I plead guilty. I have loved and used the streets of London all my life, as a cyclist, driver and pedestrian. Touch wood, I have done so without accident, blemish or insurance claim. Yet now I find myself perpetually on the wrong side of the law. Regulation has become bureaucratic and chaotic.

When I try to drive at the authorised speed of 20mph on many through roads, I am hooted at and overtaken by vans, cars, coaches and buses. And when I sit dutifully on my bike at a traffic light, I am jostled by swarms of cyclists riding through on red, furious at being treated as if they were car drivers.

As for pedestrians, walking on many pavements is like taking a ride on the dodgems. Riders of ebikes and e-scooters ignore bans and expect everyone to move out of the way.

I normally approve of anarchy. There is too much regulation everywhere. The great Dutch traffic engineer Hans Monderman boldly advocated “shared space” in cities. He wanted kerbs, road markings and traffic signals minimised and replaced by “human discipline”. All road users should navigate urban space by watching out for each other all the time. Monderman is virtually unknown in Britain, but principles similar to his were trialled with success in London’s Exhibition Road and Seven Dials. His counterintuitive ideas have been applied with remarkable success across northern Europe , with accidents falling. In 2023, 45% of Copenhageners cycled to work or school .

As a lifelong cyclist I admit to finding a certain exhilaration in riding a bike. I avoid main thoroughfares but like snaking through streets crammed with traffic, finding shortcuts through alleys and mews. But the essence of cycling is to keep moving. Hence I have to admit to sometimes doing what many London cyclists do at red lights. That is, look carefully, follow Monderman and “share” any unoccupied road space ahead by riding on.

Traffic lights can now be rendered sensitive to queues waiting at them, and change sooner to green to allow buses through. Earlier this year, a policy director for the bike hire company Lime said he wanted lights to give priority to cyclists “to improve rider behaviour and encourage more people to cycle”. This makes sense. For the time being, at pedestrian crossings, cyclists should probably just get off at a red light and cross on foot.

Investment in London’s cycle network is enabling more people to travel by bike, with the strategic cycle network now 352km long , up from 90km in 2016. It is impressive that this network was created by the same London planning authority that, 50 years ago, thought the answer to traffic planning was to build a gigantic Motorway Box .

Certainly cycling in any city is risky. The only truly safe speed is zero. But all cyclists will have their own “risk thresholds” – and the risk is largely up to them. The Highway Code’s “rules” for cyclists are near hilarious. They boil down to two words: take care.

My argument is less true when applied to ebikes, I admit. These clearly do not work in shared space, whatever Monderman might have said. Electric Santander and Lime bikes may have transformed journey times: except for the simplest train ride, they can be the fastest means of travel across town. But this comes at a price. Ebikes litter public streets with tips of abandoned machines; convenience is the mother of shambles. It cannot go on and technology must ensure bikes are properly parked.

Ebikes now come in all shapes and speeds. It is astonishing that the sleek Freesky Alaska, with its 250W engine, can be treated as if it was just another manual pedal bike. To my mind, it is blatantly a motorbike. When a delivery driver on one careers past me in Hyde Park, I wonder if I took a wrong turning. These machines must be put on the roadway where they belong.

London used to be unique among great cities in being an enjoyable place to drive. It is no longer that. The bicycle has replaced that pleasure with a new freedom – but like all freedoms, it is one that craves intelligent regulation.

articles.content:
Blondies will happily take an ice-cream filling without falling apart, and when those biscuits are infused with herbs, they also help to cut through some of the sweetness

I ce-cream sandwiches have really grown on me. I used to find them a bit tricky to eat; far too many of them had outer shells so hard they would crack a tooth, while the rest would turn to mush after a few minutes out of the freezer. Finding the balance between something thathas enough structural integrity to hold a good wedge of ice-cream but still soft enough to bite once frozen isn’t all that easy, but blondies make a very good option.

I love infusing blondies with fresh herbs to cut through some of the sweetness and add more depth. These would be great with tarragon or thyme, but today I’ve gone with rosemary for a piney, aromatic twist.

150g salted butter, plus extra for greasing 2 fresh rosemary sprigs 180g light brown sugar 1 large egg 1½ tbsp whole milk 130g plain flour ¼ tsp salt ¼ tsp bicarbonate of soda 1 litre vanilla ice-cream

For the cherries 150g cherries 30g caster sugar Squeeze of lemon juice Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and grease and line a 23cm x 33cm baking tin.

Put the butter and rosemary in a small pan and heat gently to melt. Continue cooking until the butter gets foamy and fragrant, and the milk solids turn brown. Pour everything into a bowl, remove and discard the rosemary, and cool to room temperature.

Put the sugar in a large bowl and stir in the melted butter. Whisk in the egg until smooth, followed by the milk. Sift in the flour, salt and bicarb, and stir until smooth.

Pour the batter into the prepared tin, spreading out evenly; it will be quite thin. Bake for 16-22 minutes, until the blondie looks set with crisp edges but is still a little soft in the middle. Let it cool completely in the tin, then chill in the fridge to firm up – at least six hours, but ideally overnight.

Stone and slice the cherries in half, then add to a pan with the sugar and lemon juice and bring to the boil. Cook for a few minutes until the cherries are softened and syrupy; set aside to cool completely.

Scoop the ice-cream into a large bowl, let it soften a little, then loosely fold in the cherries – try not to overmix. Cut the blondie in half widthways and scoop the ice-cream on to one half, taking it all the way to the edges. Carefully place the second blondie half on top, then wrap in clingfilm and freeze overnight, until firm.

Unwrap and trim the edges to get neat sides, then slice into bars. Serve straight away or wrap individually in baking paper and pop back in the freezer.

articles.title: The town whose council wants migrants to move in
articles.summary: Greenock wants to attract immigrants to settle in the town and reverse its declining population.
articles.content:
The population of Greenock, on Scotland's west coast, has been falling for decades

A new shop opened along Greenock's fading High Street in May. Anik African Store has brought a small corner of Nigeria to the Scottish town, selling yams, plantain, okra and catfish.

It is not the only African food shop here - there is another just metres away, responding to the area's changing population.

Five years ago, locals say, it would have been rare to see a black person in Greenock. Now hundreds of Africans and refugees have moved to the area.

The local council has in fact come up with a plan to attract even more to this corner of the west of Scotland as a means of stemming its falling population.

Scottish people "are lovely and accommodating", says Anik's owner, Christianah Omilana, who came to the UK in 2021. "Immigrants will come when there is work", she adds.

Christianah says people in Greenock have been very welcoming and friendly

The lack of work however has been a key driver of depopulation in Greenock and the wider Inverclyde area. No local authority in Scotland has been hit harder by population decline.

The number of residents in Inverclyde is 22,000 fewer than in 1981. And its current population, 78,000, is projected to fall by a further 16% over the next two decades.

Tackling the lack of people is the council's number one priority, by keeping more residents here and attracting others into the area.

It is a "lovely, friendly" town, says one of Anik's customers, Sunday, who has just moved here from Devon. He has begun a job at a hospital in Glasgow, and has come to Greenock to join his wife who works at the local hospital, Inverclyde Royal.

"If the local council can provide [jobs], everything in Greenock will change, because people [from Africa] would like to come," says Sunday.

Michael Buchanan and Adam Eley visited Greenock for the latest in a series of reports reflecting the range of challenges facing communities across the UK.

Most of Greenock's African population are working or studying in Glasgow or Paisley and have been attracted to the town by cheap housing. Many have arrived on skilled work visas, known as sponsorship, helping to bolster the health and care workforce.

Inverclyde Council's repopulation strategy is based on trying to encourage them to set down roots here, as well as attracting other legal migrants and people who've been granted refugee status to move in.

"It's a ghost town," says Tiffany, a mother of one, who we meet at a local parent and toddler group. "There's just nothing in it. There's nothing to do, there are no shops. There is no employment."

The 29-year-old moved away from Greenock to work but came back to bring up her child. Now, she says she is facing up to leaving once more.

"I'm struggling to find jobs that suit both childcare and myself. I've considered moving from here to Paisley because there is so much more to do there."

Rummage through Greenock's industrial history and you will find a distinct heritage - in the 19th Century its status as a global hub for refining sugar earned it the nickname "Sugaropolis". Thousands of ships were also built in the coastal town over a near 300-year period.

More recently, the computer manufacturer IBM employed more than 5,000 people at its campus near Greenock. But the site closed completely in 2016.

Indeed, in the past four years, a further 1,500 jobs have vanished. Amazon, EE and a string of other companies have gone elsewhere. Just this week , the local shipyard announced it was cutting about a quarter of its workforce. Meanwhile, supporters of Greenock Morton, the local football team, have set up a fighting fund to try to stave off financial collapse at the club.

The town has been left bereft - little wonder Scotland's First Minister John Swinney is due to visit this month, to hear the problems first-hand.

While health and social care roles employ many of the Africans, job opportunities for those born locally, and refugees, can be hard to find.

"When the work disappears, people disappear," says Muriel, one of dozens of elderly residents gathered at Lyle Gateway Community Cafe, a stone's throw from the High Street.

Muriel and Pamela chatted to us at a cafe housed in their local church

Between games of table tennis and cheap, hearty lunches, the group remembers a vibrant town, full of people and shops they wanted to go to.

There is a despondency now, with words like "depressing" and "empty" peppering the conversation. The pensioners are sceptical too of the council's repopulation strategy. While happy for migrants to move in, they wonder how sustainable any influx would be.

The council requires hundreds more immigrants each year just to keep the population stable.

"Where would they work?" asks Pamela. "The people in Greenock can't get work [never mind] bringing in other people."

The cafe is housed in Lyle Kirk, where Jonathan Fleming has been the Church of Scotland minister for the past five years. He feels the town's depopulation crisis at first-hand. His church does "a lot more funerals than we do weddings and baptisms," he explains. "And that shift, it's a lot more dramatic than it used to be."

The church has been supporting some Iranian refugees recently and their experience is a sobering one, says Fleming. They are desperate for paid work but can't find any.

"They're wanting to contribute to the community. They want to be independent of receiving financial aid and they're not able to do it - they're actually trapped in it, in some respects."

Church minister Jonathan Fleming says he performs "a lot more" funerals than weddings and baptisms

The number of people arriving in Inverclyde from overseas has trebled in recent times, to about 750 per year since 2023. Hundreds of African migrants have now settled in the area, as well as refugees from Ukraine, Afghanistan and several other countries, many with a positive tale to tell.

As part of its repopulation plan, the council is offering English classes for those who need them and help to access skilled employment. Schools are also supported to provide an inclusive "anti-racist education".

Mo Almalarashid arrived in Greenock in 2018 as a Syrian refugee without a word of English. He says he found a supportive community and, after studying hard, he now works as a local gym instructor. "There was always people there for me," he says.

Mo Almalarashid arrived in Greenock as a refugee in 2018, and now works as a gym instructor

There have been tensions. A local teenager was sentenced to 10 years in prison last year for planning mass murder at the local mosque. And in June, a protest outside a local hotel housing asylum seekers resulted in one woman being charged with a hate crime , and three police officers being injured.

Yet in May's Scottish Parliamentary elections, Reform UK - which campaigns strongly for lowering immigration nationally - came a distant third in Inverclyde, about 8,500 votes behind the winning SNP candidate, and despite fielding its Scottish leader in the constituency.

Other council areas will face Inverclyde's depopulation challenge in the coming years. The populations of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are all expected to begin declining within the next decade.

Stephen McCabe, who has led Inverclyde's minority Labour-led council almost exclusively since 2007, believes its repopulation plan is beginning to take effect. The population has stabilised in the past two years, he says, largely because of immigration.

Repopulation is at the heart of everything Inverclyde Council hopes to achieve, McCabe says, from housing projects and the revamping of school buildings to, perhaps most importantly, job creation.

'Just push us into the sea': The frustration of an area failed by politics

Standing on the banks of the Clyde, he sees opportunities in the maritime, renewables and defence sectors, reimagining use of the river for the 21st Century - although for that, they will need significant Scottish and UK government support.

When asked about asylum seekers, who for the most part are not permitted to work as they await Home Office decisions, McCabe acknowledges there is "an unease, no doubt about it".

While the council has "willingly" participated in a Home Office dispersal scheme - accepting more than 200 people seeking asylum - he believes the area "has been allocated a disproportionate share", with a Home Office contractor said to have bought up a number of houses in the area.

But migrants and refugees who can work are welcome in Inverclyde, McCabe says.

"Without those people, our health service would really be struggling... The refugees who have come have brought benefits to this area. They will bring ambition. They'll bring children to this area."

Greenock's population is not just shrinking, it is also ageing. The lack of children means that one nursery is closing, while older people have greater health needs.

Add in the area's high levels of deprivation, and there is increasing pressure on public services amid a shrinking tax base. Those who remain, pay more - council tax rose by almost 8% locally this year.

Matthew Quinn: Politicians should focus on "public services and ensuring we have a nice environment for people to live"

Yet you do not need to look far for a different vision for Greenock. Just 15 minutes down the road is the centre of Gourock, once similarly deprived, which has a small, thriving High Street with independent retailers, boosted by a recent £5m council investment and residents with more spending power.

Local resident Matthew Quinn, a 19-year-old former member of the Scottish Youth Parliament, says Gournock has embraced its future as a commuter town and believes other parts of Inverclyde should follow suit.

The council's focus on creating lots of jobs locally is misplaced, Matthew believes. Many people now work from home, he says, and the area's proximity to Glasgow - about 40 minutes away - should be exploited.

"If we accepted that the jobs are in Glasgow, then our focus should be on public services and ensuring we have a nice environment for people to live. Then I think we would be much more successful," he says.

"It's not that [people] are desperate to leave, it's that there's no reason to stay."

Derek Mitchell hopes to convert a disused sugar refinery into an education hub

That is a challenge that some Greenock residents are attempting to tackle, head on.

Derek Mitchell, infused with infectious positivity, is looking to convert a former sugar refinery next to an Aldi car park into a thriving hub that will teach and enthuse young people.

A focus on science, technology, engineering, arts and maths, he says, will provide them with skills for the future.

"If you build a sense of belonging, naturally and organically, people don't want to leave."

He has purchased the building as part of a group of locals, who estimate it will need £5m of investment as they continue to look for partnerships.

"A lot of people are starting to do things for themselves," he says. "They see there's potential - they're fed up of waiting."

At a time when much of the UK has concerns about immigration, Inverclyde's decision to embrace migrants and refugees makes it stand out. Its lack of people is acute, its solution, striking. Other communities will soon face a similar depopulation challenge and may look to what Greenock is trying as a possible way ahead.

The church has been supporting some Iranian refugees recently and their experience is a sobering one, says Fleming. They are desperate for paid work but can't find any.
"They're wanting to contribute to the community. They want to be independent of receiving financial aid and they're not able to do it - they're actually trapped in it, in some respects."
Church minister Jonathan Fleming says he performs "a lot more" funerals than weddings and baptisms

The number of people arriving in Inverclyde from overseas has trebled in recent times, to about 750 per year since 2023. Hundreds of African migrants have now settled in the area, as well as refugees from Ukraine, Afghanistan and several other countries, many with a positive tale to tell.

As part of its repopulation plan, the council is offering English classes for those who need them and help to access skilled employment. Schools are also supported to provide an inclusive "anti-racist education".

Mo Almalarashid arrived in Greenock in 2018 as a Syrian refugee without a word of English. He says he found a supportive community and, after studying hard, he now works as a local gym instructor. "There was always people there for me," he says.
Mo Almalarashid arrived in Greenock as a refugee in 2018, and now works as a gym instructor

There have been tensions. A local teenager was sentenced to 10 years in prison last year for planning mass murder at the local mosque. And in June, a protest outside a local hotel housing asylum seekers resulted in one woman being charged with a hate crime , and three police officers being injured.

Yet in May's Scottish Parliamentary elections, Reform UK - which campaigns strongly for lowering immigration nationally - came a distant third in Inverclyde, about 8,500 votes behind the winning SNP candidate, and despite fielding its Scottish leader in the constituency.

Other council areas will face Inverclyde's depopulation challenge in the coming years. The populations of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are all expected to begin declining within the next decade.

Stephen McCabe, who has led Inverclyde's minority Labour-led council almost exclusively since 2007, believes its repopulation plan is beginning to take effect. The population has stabilised in the past two years, he says, largely because of immigration.
Repopulation is at the heart of everything Inverclyde Council hopes to achieve, McCabe says, from housing projects and the revamping of school buildings to, perhaps most importantly, job creation.
'Just push us into the sea': The frustration of an area failed by politics

Standing on the banks of the Clyde, he sees opportunities in the maritime, renewables and defence sectors, reimagining use of the river for the 21st Century - although for that, they will need significant Scottish and UK government support.
When asked about asylum seekers, who for the most part are not permitted to work as they await Home Office decisions, McCabe acknowledges there is "an unease, no doubt about it".

While the council has "willingly" participated in a Home Office dispersal scheme - accepting more than 200 people seeking asylum - he believes the area "has been allocated a disproportionate share", with a Home Office contractor said to have bought up a number of houses in the area.
But migrants and refugees who can work are welcome in Inverclyde, McCabe says.
"Without those people, our health service would really be struggling... The refugees who have come have brought benefits to this area. They will bring ambition. They'll bring children to this area."
Greenock's population is not just shrinking, it is also ageing. The lack of children means that one nursery is closing, while older people have greater health needs.

Add in the area's high levels of deprivation, and there is increasing pressure on public services amid a shrinking tax base. Those who remain, pay more - council tax rose by almost 8% locally this year.
Matthew Quinn: Politicians should focus on "public services and ensuring we have a nice environment for people to live"

Yet you do not need to look far for a different vision for Greenock. Just 15 minutes down the road is the centre of Gourock, once similarly deprived, which has a small, thriving High Street with independent retailers, boosted by a recent £5m council investment and residents with more spending power.

Local resident Matthew Quinn, a 19-year-old former member of the Scottish Youth Parliament, says Gournock has embraced its future as a commuter town and believes other parts of Inverclyde should follow suit.

The council's focus on creating lots of jobs locally is misplaced, Matthew believes. Many people now work from home, he says, and the area's proximity to Glasgow - about 40 minutes away - should be exploited.

"If we accepted that the jobs are in Glasgow, then our focus should be on public services and ensuring we have a nice environment for people to live. Then I think we would be much more successful," he says.
"It's not that [people] are desperate to leave, it's that there's no reason to stay."
Derek Mitchell hopes to convert a disused sugar refinery into an education hub
That is a challenge that some Greenock residents are attempting to tackle, head on.
Derek Mitchell, infused with infectious positivity, is looking to convert a former sugar refinery next to an Aldi car park into a thriving hub that will teach and enthuse young people.
A focus on science, technology, engineering, arts and maths, he says, will provide them with skills for the future.
"If you build a sense of belonging, naturally and organically, people don't want to leave."
He has purchased the building as part of a group of locals, who estimate it will need £5m of investment as they continue to look for partnerships.
"A lot of people are starting to do things for themselves," he says. "They see there's potential - they're fed up of waiting."

At a time when much of the UK has concerns about immigration, Inverclyde's decision to embrace migrants and refugees makes it stand out. Its lack of people is acute, its solution, striking. Other communities will soon face a similar depopulation challenge and may look to what Greenock is trying as a possible way ahead.

articles.title: Experience: I fell 12 metres while bouldering and smashed my pelvis into pieces

One summer’s day in 2014, when I was 17, my friends and I went paddleboarding on a lake. My friend Trevor and I decided to climb one of the rocky boulders overlooking the water, and jump in. articles.content:
It was clear it was broken. I could feel the bones grinding together as the paramedics strapped me to a gurney

G rowing up in Utah, I was so active that my parents nicknamed me “The Blur”. My older siblings introduced me to rock climbing while I was still at primary school. By the time I was 15, I was hauling myself up cliff faces.

One summer’s day in 2014, when I was 17, my friends and I went paddleboarding on a lake. My friend Trevor and I decided to climb one of the rocky boulders overlooking the water, and jump in.

The rock was about 12 metres tall. I had climbed and jumped from higher. What we hadn’t counted on was a layer of moss that made the boulder slippery. Neither of us had our grippy climbing shoes with us. When I nearly fell, I thought about turning back, but I convinced myself that it was safer to keep going.

From the top, we discovered the water didn’t come right up to the boulder. Instead, there was a swathe of black volcanic rock we would have to clear first. I watched as Trevor took a run-up and hurled himself over the edge. The splash told me he’d safely made it down and into the water.

Normally I’d be excited, but the earlier slip had rattled me. Jumping still felt safer than climbing down, though. I backed up and started to run. As I reached the edge, I hesitated. It was the tiniest pause, but enough to slow my momentum. Instead of leaping outwards, I twisted sideways and started plummeting straight down.

Adrenaline and shock blurred those first moments after impact. I was about to try to move when a man appeared. He was an emergency medical technician who had been fishing nearby and had seen me fall. Suspecting a broken pelvis and spinal injuries, he held my head and neck still.

It took 30 minutes for the paramedics to reach me. It was clear my pelvis was broken. I could feel the bones grinding together as they strapped me to a gurney.

At the hospital, X-rays showed my spine was intact, but my pelvis was in pieces. I was flown by air ambulance to a better equipped hospital. Doctors there found my left arm and heel were broken too. Most dangerously, my shattered pelvic bones had cut into my organs. I was bleeding internally.

I underwent 13 hours of surgery to rebuild my pelvis with pins and metal plates. I was in hospital for two weeks before going home for six months of bed rest.

My family were amazing and gave me round-the-clock care. As an active person, it was a huge adjustment, but I just felt grateful to be alive. I also had a rota of friends who would play music and watch movies with me, which stopped me feeling sorry for myself. I’d been warned I might have permanent paralysis in my legs, but I was determined to get my life back. The fact that I was young and fit helped with my recovery. When the spinal cord swelling went down after four months, I was relieved to regain some movement.

After six months, I figured out how to pull myself out of bed and into a wheelchair. I returned to school for my senior year with some heavy-duty painkillers and a friend to push me between classes.

Ten months after the fall, I was allowed to put pressure on my feet. I had been doing hospital physical therapy, but I wasn’t convinced it was right for me. Most people with hip and pelvic injuries are elderly, whereas I was an otherwise healthy teenager. I replaced it with yoga. It was gruelling – my muscles were weak and it was a year before I could walk on my own.

I returned to the outdoors with gentle hikes, then cautiously returned to climbing – I didn’t want the accident to stop me doing something I loved. It took a couple of years to get my confidence back, but my fall made me a better climber and a stickler for safety.

I’m 29 now and a yoga teacher. People ask if I wish the accident had never happened, but the honest answer is no. It led me to this fulfilling life.

articles.title: Sydney Swans confirm no other club representatives were in Melbourne hotel room
articles.summary: Coach Dean Cox faces media after five players banned for rest of season for breaching club standards The Sydney Swans have insisted the five players suspended for failing to uphold club standards were the only club representatives present in a Melbourne hotel room in the early hours of Monday morning, as coach Dean Cox admitted “a culture isn’t perfect”. Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon were stood down by the Swans this week for breaching the club’s standards, including drinking and staying out late after last Sunday’s win over Essendon in Melbourne. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Coach Dean Cox faces media after five players banned for rest of season for breaching club standards

The Sydney Swans have insisted the five players suspended for failing to uphold club standards were the only club representatives present in a Melbourne hotel room in the early hours of Monday morning, as coach Dean Cox admitted “a culture isn’t perfect”.

Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon were stood down by the Swans this week for breaching the club’s standards, including drinking and staying out late after last Sunday’s win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Separate to that, Victoria police have also said they are investigating an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne. No one has been arrested or charged in relation to that allegation.

The Guardian does not suggest that any of the players are being accused of sexual assault, and it is reported that none of the banned players have been formally interviewed by police.

Cox, along with club captain Callum Mills, faced the media on Friday morning and the pair repeatedly knocked back questioning around the details of the night in question, citing the ongoing police investigation.

But Cox confirmed he was not in the hotel room at the centre of the scandal, after having been out for dinner with club staff earlier in the night. The coach added that he was “unaware” if there was anyone else connected to the club in the room.

“I cannot comment on what happened in the room, it is a police investigation,” Cox said. “So we’re still trying to find out information as well.”

The Swans later issued a statement to confirm their in-house investigation found only the five players who have been suspended were in the hotel room.

“The Sydney Swans can confirm that all investigations carried out by the club have consistently indicated that the only representatives of the club in the room central to the police investigation were the five players who have been stood down,” the statement read.

“We have every reason to consider that reports to the contrary are simply false.”

John Karantzis, a lawyer representing the alleged victims, had claimed earlier on Friday in an interview with 3AW Mornings there were more than five men in the room.

Cox said the club’s culture has “taken a massive hit”, and vowed to work hard to regain the community’s trust and respect.

“We all have women in our lives we deeply love. I would like to express the respect for women is of the highest priority for both myself personally and for our football club,” Cox said.

“We have some fantastic women working in our football club … and our thoughts are with them and I apologise to them, along with the women in the community, for the actions of the players. We are extremely disappointed at the actions of the players. And the sanctions imposed by the board show how serious we take these matters.

“We’re going to work … as hard as we possibly can to get the trust back from the community, to get the culture where we desire to be, where we once had been.”

Mills said he had “not seen” any teammates in his decade with the Swans engage in the sort of breach of standards for which the club sanctioned the five players.

He added he was “deeply shocked and disappointed” and apologised to the club’s AFLW players and female staff as well as “all women within the community”.

“We’re really disappointed at the actions of these five players and as a playing group we fully support the club’s decision on the sanctions handed down,” Mills said, adding the five players had “let us down”.

The club’s AFL captain said he had spoken to the suspended players and described the conversation as “extremely hard”. He denied there was a “rift” within the playing group and refused to comment on whether he would welcome the players back to the team amid the ongoing police investigation.

Mills said he had addressed the AFLW players and “acknowledged their pain and I deeply apologised for the actions of a few within our group”.

Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy said later on Friday the club had “taken a reputational hit”.

McEvoy added the club was “absolutely united” across the AFL and AFLW programs, and said “absolutely, yes” when asked whether she would want to have input in the five players returning to the club.

The five players’ breach of the Swans’ standards and the media storm that has followed have taken the spotlight away from what was meant to be a momentous occasion for the club.

Plans to heavily promote the AFLW and AFL teams playing their first double header at the SCG on Sunday have largely been put on hold.

“This week was supposed to be a really big day for our football club and the W program, so to be able to get that support – we feel it a lot, we’ve had a lot of messages through social media – and the best way to support us in this moment is get to the game on Sunday and hopefully break a record crowd,” McEvoy said.

articles.title: Rain to stop in time for weekend as sun returns
articles.summary: The heavy downpours that have caused flash flooding will ease during Friday with sunshine returning for the weekend. But there are some chilly nights in store, as Ben Rich explains.
articles.content:
High pressure is set to build across the UK over the next few days bringing drier weather for the weekend.

Heavy downpours have brought rain to parts in need this week - albeit with some flash flooding - but these are set to ease.

Many areas will see sunny spells across Saturday and Sunday with daytime temperatures climbing again, perhaps to above the August average in parts of the south of England.

Friday will bring the chance of further heavy showers, particularly in England and Wales where a few could still be thundery.

However most parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland will be dry for much of the time.

Northerly winds will be fairly brisk around some coasts, and will make it feel rather cool.

Temperatures are set to peak at 12C in northern Scotland, where it could get up to 21C across southern England, somewhat below the average for August.

If temperatures fail to reach 25C anywhere in the UK - as looks likely - it will be the first time that has happened since 29 June.

Friday night will be a notably chilly night - and may come as a shock to the system.

Temperatures are expected to fall to 3-4C in some rural parts of Scotland and northern England.

Average night time temperatures in August range from 8C in northern Scotland to 15C in southern England

Chilly nights will continue to be a feature over the weekend but with more sunshine and lighter winds, daytime temperatures will climb.

By Sunday, afternoon highs will reach 16-20C in Scotland and Northern Ireland, with 19-25C predicted for England and Wales.

A few scattered light showers are possible in the north and west of the UK but the vast majority will be dry, with a mix of patchy cloud and sunny spells.

The heavy downpours of the last few days brought some localised flash flooding but have not been enough to alleviate the ongoing drought situation.

On Thursday, the National Drought Group announced that it will begin meeting weekly - instead of monthly, as usual - to coordinate the ongoing response.

Over two-thirds of England is in drought - along with all of Wales - and officials say the situation is still intensifying despite this week's rain.

Drought will only be declared as over once reservoirs, rivers and groundwater stocks are replenished. This will only happen after months of sustained, significant rainfall.

The outlook for the next few weeks looks rather mixed with rain set to return next week, but the ongoing chance of further hot spells during September.

There is a lot of uncertainty in the long-range forecast and you can keep up to date with your local prospects on the BBC Weather website and app .

articles.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 19: Sunderland
articles.summary: Sunderland fans hope Régis Le Bris and his talented squad can continue to surprise the pundits and Opta Guardian writers’ predicted position: 14th (NB: this is not necessarily Louise Taylor’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips) Last season’s position: 7th Continue reading...
articles.content:
Sunderland fans hope Régis Le Bris and his talented squad can continue to surprise the pundits and Opta

Guardian writers’ predicted position: 14th (NB: this is not necessarily Louise Taylor’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

After finishing seventh last season, Sunderland go into the new campaign engaged in continental combat for the first time since a brief adventure in the old Cup Winners’ Cup in 1973-74. Will their startling upward trajectory under Régis Le Bris continue or will they succumb to the dreaded second-season syndrome? No one is quite sure.

While many like to highlight Sunderland’s relegation-level XG statistics last season, it is important to note that a steadily improving squad lost six players to the Africa Cup of Nations in the winter. Moreover, no key player has been sold this summer, team spirit is superb and pre-season performances have been reassuringly convincing. Le Bris accepts coping with Thursday night football will be a challenge for a club that played in League One as recently as 2022, but insists it is something to be enjoyed rather than feared.

It helps that Sunderland still have their captain, Granit Xhaka, controlling midfield. If Xhaka’s decision to recommit to life at the Stadium of Light despite serious interest from Chelsea lifted the pre-season mood, further optimism is provided by the presence of high-calibre individuals, including the fans’ favourite Enzo Le Fée, Chris Rigg, Robin Roefs, Noah Sadiki and Nordi Mukiele, in a versatile squad containing several players comfortable in assorted positions. Brian Brobbey is the sort of robust centre-forward few defenders enjoy marking. “We are growing together,” says Le Bris. “We’ve shown the team is strong.”

Sunderland are majority-owned by the 29-year-old Swiss-French businessman and trust fund billionaire Kyril Louis-Dreyfus. The son of the late former Marseille owner Robert Louis-Dreyfus has a 64%stake in the club while the remaining 36% is held by the Uruguayan businessman and politician Juan Sartori. The strong relationship between Le Bris and the director of football, Florent Ghisolfi, has helped ensure on-pitch stability, although the past year has brought considerable off-field change, with several key executives replaced as Sunderland’s commercial strategy pivots in a more international direction. While the team toured the United States this summer, other marketing efforts have been concentrated on Africa, with a lucrative, and controversial, front-of-shirt sponsorship with Visit Ghana close to being finalised. More locally, the regeneration of the area adjacent to the Stadium of Light is transforming a post-industrial landscape.

If Louis-Dreyfus initially attracted a degree of suspicion and scepticism on taking the helm in 2021, he has earned the trust of the fanbase. Supporters were particularly impressed that the owner contacted Xhaka and convinced the Switzerland captain to join from Bayer Leverkusen last summer. Less positively, a creep towards increased corporate hospitality, allied to a divisive new club membership scheme, has polarised season-ticket holders.

Le Bris enjoys a spot of close-season surfing on the beaches of his native Brittany, so it is perhaps appropriate that the 50-year-old rode a footballing wave last season. His 2025 Championship playoff winners hit the Premier League ground running and proved they could last the course. Along the way, Le Bris parked his tanks on Newcastle’s front lawn by choreographing two league wins over their rivals. Le Bris holds a doctorate in physiology and biomechanics and a diploma in the mental training of elite athletes. He spent a decade as a highly regarded youth coach at Lorient before taking charge of the first team in 2022, with his love of trigonometry underpinning a coaching philosophy that views football as fundamentally being about triangles.

Sunderland tried and failed to sign Thomas Meunier from Lille a year ago, but patience has been rewarded. At the time of writing, the 34-year-old free transfer is the sole summer signing – quite a contrast to the 14 new faces 12 months ago – but at least two more new recruits are expected before the window closes. Meunier, who has 83 Belgium caps and played at the World Cup, will compete with Mukiele and Trai Hume at right-back. The experience he has acquired throughout a career involving stints at Paris Saint-Germain and Borussia Dortmund should prove useful in the Europa League.

If matches were decided by Opta’s expected points metric, Sunderland would have been relegated last season. Instead they are preparing for a Europa League campaign after finishing 11 places higher than the XG figures implied they deserved. It was a wider margin between statistical performance and outcome than any other team in Europe’s big five leagues experienced, for good or bad.

Tom Proctor, the son of Sunderland’s first-team coach and former forward, Michael Proctor, is only 17 and starting his second year as an academy scholar.He was included in the first-team squad for the pre-season tour of the United States. Proctor has impressed with his technical ability, awareness and eye for goal. With the squad set to be stretched by Europa League involvement, it will be no surprise if a player who joined Sunderland’s academy at the age of six makes a competitive first-team debut this season.

Sunderland had 12 players at the World Cup, more than Real Madrid, and such visibility delighted executives charged with growing the club’s commercial revenue streams. Wilson Isidor scored Haiti’s first World Cup goal since 1974 while Brobbey struck three times for the Netherlands. The entire group has since been joined by Meunier, who represented Belgium in the United States.

articles.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for as the new season kicks off
articles.summary: Manchester United’s new-look midfield, Ipswich’s ambition is tested and Kevin Keegan tributes at Newcastle While Myles Lewis-Skelly looks likely to remain at the Emirates , the same can’t be said for Ethan Nwaneri. Ed Aarons Arsenal v Coventry City, Friday 8pm (all times BST) Hull City v Manchester United, Saturday 12.30pm Everton v Crystal Palace, Saturday 3pm Ipswich Town v Sunderland, Saturday 3pm Nottingham Forest v Leeds, Saturday 3pm Brighton v Aston Villa, Sunday 2pm Manchester City v Bournemouth, Sunday 2pm Continue reading...
articles.content:
Manchester United’s new-look midfield, Ipswich’s ambition is tested and Kevin Keegan tributes at Newcastle

While Myles Lewis-Skelly looks likely to remain at the Emirates , the same can’t be said for Ethan Nwaneri. The 19-year-old was outstanding in his breakthrough season for Arsenal in 2024-25 but barely featured last season and was sent on loan to Marseille. That didn’t really work out and Arsenal are now exploring another temporary move to ensure Nwaneri gets regular football this season. Milan, RB Leipzig, Dortmund and Fulham are all thought to be interested, with Nwaneri unlikely to feature on the bench for Friday’s opener against Coventry as a result. Whether Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus are available remains to be seen as Arsenal attempt to find suitors for the Brazil duo. Ed Aarons

Manchester United’s summer transfer business has focused on recruiting in central midfield. It will be interesting to see who Michael Carrick selects in two key roles for the first game of the season. Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans have been present for more of pre-season than Kobbie Mainoo, who did not play a minute for England at the World Cup and was a late returner to Carrington after a holiday. Carlos Baleba surely will not have arrived in time to start at Hull. Mainoo is in the best position in the long term but if Carrick decides to ease him into the season, it would be intriguing to see how Santos and Tielemans team up, the stress test for a new partnership that could provide the perfect balance of defensive awareness and ability to move the team up the pitch. Will Unwin

Neither club has enjoyed a particularly scintillating summer of transfer activity but combined to make headlines with a swap deal between Dwight McNeil and Brennan Johnson. The pair will face one another – and their former clubs - on the first weekend of the season, eager to prove what their worth to their new teams. McNeil was rarely a regular on Merseyside but had a positive second half to last season, ironically after a move to Crystal Palace fell through at the last minute. Johnson did not settle at Selhurst Park, unable to crack the code that would get him into the starting lineup on a weekly basis. A fresh start should reinvigorate the duo and there is no better way to further boost the mood than beating a former employer. WU

Ipswich clearly learned a lot from what Sunderland did a year ago, as they went out and bought a lot of players. The Black Cats quickly moulded their 19 acquisitions into a successful unit but at least they had the positive of a head coach in Régis Le Bris who had his feet under the table. Gary O’Neil is the new man at Portman Road and he has 12 signings – at time of writing – to potentially use for the opener. The record arrival, Emersonn, who has moved to Portman Road from Toulouse, is the most eye-catching of those who have been acquired. The Brazilian has an underwhelming career goalscoring record and a few question marks hanging over his head. Even though it is their first game, Ipswich need to pick up points at home, and to do so require a striker who can cause problems for defenders. How quickly Emersonn adapts will be critical for the Tractor Boys’ success this year. WU

August is the season for debuts and no one will be more satisfied than Oliver Glasner when Ousmane Diomande steps over the white line at the City Ground. Glasner wanted the Ivorian centre-back to replace Marc Guéhi at Crystal Palace, six months before the England defender departed for Manchester City . Diomande, a £34m buy from Sporting, is expected to line up in a back three for Nottingham Forest against Leeds, when the Austria midfielder Xaver Schlager, who played for Glasner at Wolfsburg, could also make his Forest bow. Diomande is a quick and physical defender but another aspect of his appeal is his aerial power at set pieces. “They’ve both played Champions League football and they are used to competing for titles,” said Glasner. “They can add this winning mentality.” Ben Fisher

Cristian Romero has taken his maverick brand of defending to Atlético Madrid, upsetting neutral Premier League watchers. His compatriot Marcos Senesi has arrived to shore up things at the back as Roberto De Zerbi desperately tries to steer Spurs away from a third straight season of battling relegation. The all-action Romero had his qualities as a leader and defender but never felt dependable, which is what most want from a centre-back and captain. Senesi impressed during his time at Bournemouth, rarely making headlines but proving himself a calm presence at the back. The Argentinian is good on the ball and will be more adventurous in possession than his countryman. He is yet to be sent off in three seasons as a Premier League player – Romero was dismissed twice in 2025-26 alone, not to mention a one-match ban and a fine for his behaviour towards a referee. His calmness will improve Spurs. WU

It is surely not how Unai Emery envisaged the countdown to Aston Villa’s season-opener at Brighton on Sunday – and certainly not as he enjoyed the afterglow from the club’s Europa League triumph over Freiburg in May. The manager has an extraordinary number of problems. Take the midfield where the new signings João Gomes and Johan Manzambi are injury doubts. Note: Amadou Onana is a long-term casualty while Youri Tielemans has been sold. It goes on. Emery is about to lose Ezri Konsa to Arsenal – in a summer where Villa have also sold Morgan Rogers and Lucas Digne. They are trying to move on Emi Martínez, while the future of Ollie Watkins is uncertain, with Al-Hilal circling. For the cherry on top, the rampaging 17-year-old striker Brian Madjo is a fitness concern. Emery’s teamsheet will be very interesting. Will he pitch the new goalkeeper, Zion Suzuki, who only signed on Wednesday, straight in? David Hytner

Is Enzo Maresca already under pressure after Manchester City’s 3-0 schooling by Arsenal in the Community Shield? Maybe not, but if the Italian’s new team go down at home to Bournemouth on Sunday, you do not have to be a soothsayer to picture the scrutiny that will follow. Maresca and City are enduring a difficult transfer window, with Rodri’s departure to Barcelona the headline, a dizzying blow that has to be shaken off. The new Bournemouth coach, Marco Rose, has faced City six times in the Champions League with Leipzig and Mönchengladbach, and is sure to order his visitors to go for the jugular at the Etihad. City are vulnerable but Maresca can remedy this with a win of any sort. This, after all, is the job many felt he was the obvious choice for. Jamie Jackson

Kevin Keegan was supposed to have been the guest of honour at St James’ Park on Sunday, but his death from cancer in July means this meeting of two of his old clubs will turn into a tribute to one of English football’s enduring heroes . Keegan’s family will be present to witness an outpouring of love for the former Liverpool and Newcastle forward and (twice) Magpies manager. Once the game kicks off, all eyes will be on Alexander Isak, a St James’ Park old boy whose decision to force a £125m move to Anfield last summer did not go down well on Tyneside. The Sweden striker, making his first return to Newcastle, has much to prove at Liverpool, and now has a new head coach to impress in Andoni Iraola. Newcastle too have a new face in the home dugout, where Matthias Jaissle will occupy the technical area for so long inhabited by Eddie Howe. Louise Taylor

Real Madrid’s two head coaches from last season meet at Craven Cottage, with the focus on Xabi Alonso, rather than Álvaro Arbeloa. The Fulham man, however, may have more to prove in the Premier League. His managerial career has been less prominent than that of his Basque rival – and he has clearly insisted on snapping up talent from the Bernabéu. Gonzalo García and César Palacios have made the trip over from the Spanish capital with Arbeloa. It shows great faith from the former Liverpool defender but it does put extra pressure on the trio, their fates now permanently intertwined. All three need a positive start to show they merit being in the Premier League. Otherwise, it would be very easily to criticise them individually and collectively. WU

articles.title: European playoffs: Rangers scrape first-leg win as Brighton draw in Norway
articles.summary: 10-man Rangers hang on for 1-0 win against Jablonec Tromsø 0-0 Brighton; Hearts 2-2 Rapid Vienna Ryan Naderi’s second-half strike gave an unconvincing Rangers a narrow 1-0 win in the first leg of their Conference League playoff tie against Czech side Jablonec at Ibrox. Derek McInnes got his first win as Rangers manager at the fifth time of asking with a 5-1 thumping of St Mirren on Sunday but there was regression in the goalless first half which brought boos at the interval whistle. articles.content:
Ryan Naderi’s second-half strike gave an unconvincing Rangers a narrow 1-0 win in the first leg of their Conference League playoff tie against Czech side Jablonec at Ibrox. Derek McInnes got his first win as Rangers manager at the fifth time of asking with a 5-1 thumping of St Mirren on Sunday but there was regression in the goalless first half which brought boos at the interval whistle.

The Govan side pepped up after the break and Naderi opened the scoring from close range in the 50th minute but in the 78th minute the substitute Cammy Devlin was sent off – minutes after coming off the bench – for a high tackle on Jiri Slama to leave Rangers to see out the game with 10 men.

Fabian Hürzeler, admitted: “It’s not the result we hoped for,” after Brighton were held to a frustrating goalless draw against Tromsø in Norway. The Seagulls, who open the new domestic campaign against Aston Villa on Sunday, created several good chances but could not find a way past the Tromsø keeper Jakob Haugaard.

The winger Ibrahim Osman – making his Brighton debut after three loan spells away – looked particularly lively during the first half. Tromsø then almost snatched a late winner on the break, but the defender Isak Vadebu sent his shot wide as the tie went into next week’s second leg at the Amex Stadium all square.

Hearts ’ head coach, Wouter Vrancken, hopes James Wilson’s stunning goal in the 2-2 Conference League draw with Rapid Vienna is a sign of things to come from the youngster. He drilled in an unstoppable drive from 30 yards just moments after coming on as the hosts took the lead in the playoff first leg.

“He’s a young lad so for sure it will be extra special. Let’s hope he can make the next steps,” Vrancken said.

Wilson’s effort marked an impressive turnaround after Josh McPade cancelled out Serge-Philippe Raux-Yao’s first-half header. However, Rapid scrambled in a late equaliser through Nikolaus Wumbrand to ensure the tie remains on a knife edge ahead of next week’s return leg.

David Gray, the Hibernian head coach, savoured “a massive performance and a massive result” as his side kept themselves on course to reach the main phase with a spirited 0-0 draw in Belgium against Gent .

For the second Thursday night in a row, Hibs ground out a stalemate on foreign soil after they eliminated Shkendija in North Macedonia last week. It could have been even better for them if Owen Elding’s 15th-minute penalty had not been saved by Davy Roef.

Motherwell made a whirlwind start at home to Freiburg , with Regan Charles-Cook sidefooting in Emmanuel Longelo’s cutback after just 73 seconds. But Matthias Ginter headed Freiburg level on 27 minutes and netted a second from the spot, after Martin Moormann was shown a straight red card on 65 minutes via a video assistant referee review.

The substitute Keisuke Goto added a third with a stoppage-time header to leave the Scottish side with a 3-1 deficit mountain to climb in Germany next Thursday.

The Northern Irish champions, Larne , took a big step towards the league phase after a 2-0 win at 10-man Lincoln Red Imps .

The match looked set to finish goalless in Gibraltar after Red Imps had held firm following Yussef Flalhi’s 29th-minute red card. However, visiting Larne made their pressure pay when Paul O’Neill struck with five minutes left before fellow substitute Kevin O’Hara’s stoppage-time breakaway goal ensured Gary Haveron’s side will have a cushion ahead of the second leg at Inver Park.

Shamrock were held to a 1-1 draw at home by the Finnish side KuPS after they conceded an 85th-minute equaliser. The former Sheffield United full-back Enda Stevens put the Irish side ahead after 49 minutes, but they were denied a precious victory when the one-time Charlton youngster Piotr Parzyszek levelled late on at Tallaght Stadium.

In the Europa League , Mohamed Salah played all 90 minutes of his home debut as Trabzonspor hosted Ferencvaros , but the Hungarian side won 1-0 and their Turkish opponents had Chibuike Nwaiwu sent off in added time.

articles.title: Ronaldinho, 46, on mission of love and happiness – and maybe goals – at Serie C’s Ravenna

articles.content:
Brazilian legend pledges excitement at his unveiling for a comeback that is winning over initially disbelieving fans

I t seemed like a joke, a hoax, when at 10pm on 19 June, Ravenna broke the news of Ronaldinho’s signing . The Brazilian, a former Ballon d’Or winner and one of the most recognisable figures in world football, had played his last official match in 2015 for Fluminense; a professional signing in Serie C at 46 years of age seemed unrealistic, to say the least. With football’s attention taken by the World Cup, the game was shocked by this bolt from the blue. For the most part, it remained in disbelief.

There was much discussion, in the city and around the world, about the real value of this operation, and we talked about it too, speaking with the mayor, the fans, and the president of Ravenna, Ignazio Cipriani, scion of the family known globally for Harry’s Bar, who is giving his city much more than a dream.

A dream that materialised, dispelling any doubts, at 11.50am on Thursday, when Ronaldinho , in a floral shirt and Bermuda shorts, with his now-familiar flat cap on his head, walked down the steps of the private jet that brought him from Milan Linate to the runway of Forlì airport. It is all true, all real. From there, he went on to the customary medical, like a true footballer. Ronaldinho is becoming a partner in the Ravenna club, as explained by the president, but he will also do his part on the pitch, with the dream of scoring the final goal of his career in the yellow-and-red jersey.

Then came the quick press conference, organised by the ownership at the Monaldina, the historic residence of the Gardini-Ferruzzi entrepreneurial family, the maternal dynasty from which Cipriani descends. There were few questions and hushed answers, very few words carefully chosen by Ronaldinho, who with his customary smile and gentle manners truly seems to have stepped back in time.

“The Milan derby is the most beautiful memory of my previous Italian experience,” began the former Barcelona and Milan No 10, before clarifying what drove him to Romagna: “Friendship and passion are the keys that brought me back here.”

He then clarified his goals in Ravenna: “To help, to excite the other players, and to have a spectacular season. To win, if possible.” Regarding his possible presence on the pitch, he explained: “If a goal comes, my experience in Ravenna will become even more beautiful, but whether I will actually play will be decided by the president and the coach.”

What does he think of the enthusiasm of Ravenna, a city that has literally gone crazy for him? Ronaldinho smiled and replied: “I just arrived, but I have a great desire to live this experience with the whole city.” His mission, he had already declared, is to bring happiness and love.

Echoing his words and capturing the essence of the city’s excitement was Ariedo Braida. Almost enunciating every word, the veteran executive summarised the operation with a striking remark: “We have the magic of football in Ravenna, what more could we ask for?”

The former Milan and Barcelona director also recalled the opinion expressed by Kevin-Prince Boateng in 2016, according to which Ronaldinho holds the top spot in a ranking that also includes Pelé, Maradona, Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo.

Closing the circle was Cipriani himself, who revealed the behind-the-scenes of the miracle, after clarifying: “Ronaldinho is in shape.” When asked how he convinced the Brazilian champion, the answer was identical to that of the player: “Friendship and passion.” Cipriani then confirmed Ronaldinho’s entry as a shareholder in Ravenna FC, insisting on the profound meaning of the corporate move: “It’s not just about marketing, it’s not just international visibility. It is the chance to create a new enthusiasm around the club and the yellow-and-red jersey.”

Then the party began, organised in grand style on a stage set up on the beach at Marina di Ravenna, featuring the presentation of the entire Ravenna squad. The club’s president does not hide the ambition of a rapid climb to Serie B, with his sights set on the top flight. The star of the event, needless to say, was the Brazilian star, who for the first time presented himself before his new people, those Ravenna fans who back in June were curious, sceptical, or in disbelief.

Every doubt was dispelled on the beach of the ancient Byzantine capital, which today, with the arrival of the former Ballon d’Or winner, can truly dream big.

In living memory, the Romagnol city has never been talked about so much all over the world.

The fans didn’t just show up on the beach to celebrate their new idol, they also did so at the box office: the “Ronaldinho effect” has led to over 2,700 season tickets sold for Ravenna’s Serie C campaign, which kicks off on Monday in Reggio Emilia.

Ronaldinho, as confirmed by Cipriani, will not take part in the away match, but the fans hope to soon see him wearing the No 10 jersey, which was handed to him upon his arrival in Ravenna by the head coach, Andrea Mandorlini.

“Thank you very much,” are the words Ronaldinho dedicated to his celebrating people, while a child climbing the scaffolding of the giant screen shouted: “I saw him!”

He saw him at 46 years old, they had told him stories about him. Perhaps he will see him play again. This is the magic of football.

articles.title: Can Aryna Sabalenka find a way to repair her collapsed form? | Tumaini Carayol
articles.summary: With one semi-final in her last seven tournaments, the coming months will define the next stage of her career Towards the end of a messy first set tie-break late on Wednesday, Aryna Sabalenka wildly sprayed another painfully nervous backhand before slamming her racket to the ground.
